## About PinkDefense
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/about/

PinkDefense is a Houston law practice and affiliate of Walter J. Pink & Associates, PC and Pink Law Enterprises, continuing a 50-year Pink family legacy in Texas courts.

PinkDefense is the Houston criminal defense practice of attorney Ishmael G. A. Pink and an affiliate of Walter J. Pink & Associates, PC and Pink Law Enterprises. We defend clients in state and federal court and in white-collar investigations across Harris County and Fort Bend County. Personal injury matters are handled through PinkInjury.com, and business and transactional matters through PinkBusiness.com.

## The Legacy of Walter Jerome Pink
Our story begins with Walter Jerome Pink, a civil rights activist and heavyweight boxer once known in the ring as "The Tobasco Kid." While working as a college professor at age 28, he watched a student arrested unlawfully and saw his wife, Betty Pink, face discrimination. He decided the most effective way to fight injustice was inside the courtroom.

Over more than 30 years of practice he handled more than 20,000 criminal cases, tried more than 600 criminal trials, and received formal recognition from the Texas Senate. The firm he founded in 1972 became a multi-generational Houston institution.

## Three Generations
- Augustin T. Pink, his son, has practiced since 1992 and leads criminal defense strategy, with more than 30 years in Texas and federal courts and matters handled in Africa and South America.
- Clement B. Pink, his son, focuses on civil litigation and personal injury and has secured more than $25 million in settlements for clients.
- Ishmael G. A. Pink, his grandson and a two-time University of Texas graduate, founded PinkDefense to carry the family's trial-first approach into criminal and white-collar defense.

## What We Handle
- Criminal defense: felonies and misdemeanors, DWI, drug, violent crime, family violence, weapons, sex offenses, federal charges, expunctions and appeals.
- White-collar: fraud, embezzlement, securities, health care fraud, money laundering, and federal investigations.

The family of firms has also represented businesses and members of the entertainment and sports industries.

## What We Do Not Handle
To make sure you get the right help, note that we do not handle immigration, bankruptcy, estate planning or probate, patents or trademarks, family law, Social Security disability, or tax disputes. We are glad to point you toward someone who does.

## Where We Practice
Our office is at 1717 St. James Place, Suite 690, Houston, TX 77056. We serve Houston, Harris County, Fort Bend County (including Sugar Land, Missouri City, Richmond, Rosenberg, Stafford, Fulshear and Needville), Katy, and surrounding communities, and we appear in the federal courts of the Southern District of Texas.

## Frequently Asked Questions
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/frequently-asked-question-faq/

Answers to common questions about criminal defense, DWI, bonds, expunctions and fees in Houston and Fort Bend County.

Below are answers to questions we hear most often from clients in Houston, Sugar Land, Richmond and across Harris and Fort Bend Counties. For advice about your specific situation, call (832) 979-0882.

Q: Do you handle cases in both Harris County and Fort Bend County?
A: Yes. We regularly appear at the Harris County Criminal Justice Center in downtown Houston and the Fort Bend County Justice Center in Richmond, as well as municipal courts in Houston, Sugar Land, Missouri City, Stafford, Rosenberg and Katy, and federal court in the Southern District of Texas.

Q: How is PinkDefense related to Walter J. Pink & Associates?
A: PinkDefense is an affiliate of Walter J. Pink & Associates, PC and Pink Law Enterprises, the Pink family of firms founded by civil rights attorney Walter Jerome Pink more than 50 years ago.

Q: How much does a criminal defense lawyer cost?
A: For most criminal cases we quote a flat fee after a free consultation, so you know the cost up front. The fee depends on the charge, the county, and whether the case is likely to go to trial.

Q: What should I do right after an arrest?
A: Stay calm, do not discuss the facts with police, jail staff, or other inmates, and do not post about the case. Ask for a lawyer and call us at (832) 979-0882. In a DWI arrest, you generally have only 15 days to request an ALR hearing to protect your license.

Q: Do you handle personal injury or business matters?
A: Those matters are handled by our affiliated practices. For personal injury, visit PinkInjury.com. For transactional and business matters, visit PinkBusiness.com.

Q: Will I have to go to court?
A: In felony cases you must generally appear at each setting. In many misdemeanor cases your attorney can handle some settings, but you must still appear when the court requires it. We tell you in advance which dates you must attend.

Q: Can my case be dismissed?
A: Sometimes. Dismissals can result from suppression of evidence, insufficient proof, a complaining witness who does not support the case, or completion of a pretrial intervention program. We evaluate those paths at the start.

Q: What is deferred adjudication?
A: A form of community supervision where the judge does not find you guilty. If you complete the conditions, the case is dismissed, and you may be eligible for an order of nondisclosure. It still counts as a prior for some purposes, so it must be weighed carefully.

Q: Can I get my arrest record cleared?
A: If your case was dismissed, no-billed or ended in acquittal, you may qualify for an expunction. Certain deferred adjudication and some convictions may qualify for nondisclosure. See Expunctions & Record Sealing.

Q: Do you speak to my family if I am in jail?
A: With your permission, yes. We can coordinate with family about bond, court dates and documents we need.

## Houston & Fort Bend County DWI Lawyer
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/

Houston and Fort Bend County DWI defense lawyer. First and repeat DWI, felony DWI, intoxication assault, ALR hearings and license protection. Call (832) 979-0882.

A driving while intoxicated arrest starts two cases at once: a criminal case in Harris County or Fort Bend County court, and an administrative license suspension through the Texas Department of Public Safety. You generally have 15 days from the arrest to request an Administrative License Revocation (ALR) hearing, so the clock starts immediately.

Under Texas Penal Code § 49.04, a person is intoxicated if they have lost the normal use of their mental or physical faculties because of alcohol, drugs, or a combination, or if they have a blood or breath alcohol concentration of 0.08 or more. The State can try to prove either theory, which means a DWI can be charged even when a test result is below 0.08 or when no test was taken.

## How a Houston DWI Case Unfolds
Arrests on I-610, I-10, I-69/US-59, Beltway 8, the Grand Parkway and SH-6 are made by HPD, the Harris County Sheriff's Office, county constables, Fort Bend County deputies, Sugar Land and Missouri City police, and DPS troopers. Most cases involve a breath test on an Intoxilyzer 9000 or a blood draw under a search warrant, especially during "no refusal" enforcement periods.

## Our DWI Defense
We review the legal basis for the stop, the officer's field sobriety testing, the breath-test operator's certification and the instrument's records, and the blood-draw warrant and lab analysis. Our goal is a dismissal, an acquittal, or a reduction that protects your license, job and record.

---

## First DWI
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/first-dwi/

What a first DWI means in Houston and Fort Bend County: penalties, license suspension, deferred adjudication and how to fight the charge.

A first DWI in Texas is usually a Class B misdemeanor. Even so, it carries a mandatory minimum of 72 hours in jail if jail is imposed (six days if an open container was in the vehicle), a fine of up to $2,000, a possible license suspension, and a state traffic fine of $3,000 after conviction ($6,000 if the alcohol concentration was 0.16 or more).

## Options for First-Time Offenders
Many first-time clients avoid jail entirely. Depending on the facts and the court, outcomes can include dismissal, reduction to a non-DWI offense such as obstructing a highway, community supervision, or deferred adjudication, which became available for most DWIs in 2019. A first DWI conviction or deferred adjudication may later qualify for an order of nondisclosure.

## Do Not Miss the ALR Deadline
Your license can be suspended for 90 days for a failed test or 180 days for a refusal unless you request an ALR hearing within 15 days of arrest. That hearing also gives us an early chance to question the arresting officer under oath.

---

## Second DWI
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/second-dwi/

Second DWI charges in Houston and Fort Bend County: Class A penalties, mandatory jail, ignition interlock and defense strategies.

A second DWI is a Class A misdemeanor under Penal Code § 49.09(a), punishable by 30 days to one year in county jail and a fine of up to $4,000. Judges must require an ignition interlock device as a condition of bond, and a conviction triggers a longer license suspension and a higher state traffic fine.

The State has to prove the prior conviction with proper records, and it must still prove the new DWI beyond a reasonable doubt. We examine both. A second arrest is also not automatically a "second DWI" if the earlier case ended in dismissal or acquittal.

Probation is possible for a second offense, often with conditions such as an interlock, alcohol monitoring, counseling and community service. When the evidence is weak, we push for dismissal or a reduction that avoids the repeat-offender penalties.

---

## Third or Subsequent DWI
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/third-or-subsequent-dwi/

Felony third DWI charges in Harris and Fort Bend County: prison ranges, probation eligibility, and how we challenge prior convictions.

A third DWI, or any DWI with two prior DWI convictions, is a third-degree felony under Penal Code § 49.09(b). The punishment range is two to ten years in prison and a fine of up to $10,000. A conviction is a permanent felony record.

Felony DWI cases are filed in district court. The State must prove both prior convictions with certified judgments and fingerprints or other identity evidence. Defects in those records are a common and powerful defense. We also test the new arrest itself: the stop, the field sobriety tests, and the chemical testing.

Probation is available in many felony DWI cases, frequently with an ignition interlock, continuous alcohol monitoring, treatment, and a period of jail time as a condition. Specialty treatment courts may also be an option for eligible clients.

---

## Felony DWI
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/felony-dwi/

Felony DWI charges in Houston: third DWI, DWI with a child passenger, intoxication assault and intoxication manslaughter.

Several situations turn a DWI into a felony in Texas:

- Two or more prior DWI convictions (third-degree felony).
- A passenger younger than 15 (state jail felony under § 49.045).
- Serious bodily injury to another person (intoxication assault, third-degree felony).
- A death (intoxication manslaughter, second-degree felony).

Felony DWI cases are indicted by a grand jury and heard in district court. Before indictment, we can sometimes present information to prosecutors or the grand jury that changes the charging decision. After indictment, we examine accident reconstruction, blood evidence, and causation, which are often the weakest links in the State's case.

---

## DWI With a 0.15 BAC or Higher
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/dwi-with-0-15-bac/

High-BAC DWI in Texas: Class A charges for 0.15 BAC or more, ignition interlock requirements, and challenging blood and breath results.

Since 2015, a first DWI with an alcohol concentration of 0.15 or more at the time of testing has been a Class A misdemeanor, carrying up to one year in jail and a $4,000 fine. If probation is granted, the court must require an ignition interlock. Deferred adjudication is not available when the result is 0.15 or higher.

Because the enhancement depends entirely on the number, the reliability of that number matters. We examine whether the breath instrument was properly maintained and operated, whether the two breath samples agreed, and, for blood, whether the sample was correctly collected, preserved, stored and analyzed. Retrograde extrapolation, or estimating BAC at the time of driving, is often scientifically unsupported.

---

## DWI With a Child Passenger
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/dwi-with-child-passenger/

DWI with a child passenger under 15 is a state jail felony in Texas. Learn the penalties, CPS concerns, and defenses.

Driving while intoxicated with a passenger younger than 15 is a state jail felony under Penal Code § 49.045, even on a first arrest. It carries 180 days to two years in a state jail facility, a fine of up to $10,000, and a license suspension. Officers in these cases can seek a mandatory blood draw.

These arrests often bring a report to the Department of Family and Protective Services. Coordinating the criminal defense with any CPS investigation protects both your freedom and your family. We challenge the intoxication evidence, the child's age documentation, and the legality of the stop and any blood draw.

---

## Intoxication Assault
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/intoxication-assault/

Intoxication assault charges in Houston and Fort Bend County: third-degree felony penalties, causation defenses and accident reconstruction.

Intoxication assault under Penal Code § 49.07 is causing serious bodily injury to another person by accident or mistake while intoxicated in a vehicle, boat, or aircraft, or while operating an amusement ride. It is a third-degree felony, and the penalty increases when the injured person is a peace officer, firefighter, or emergency medical worker on duty or when the injury causes a traumatic brain injury leading to a persistent vegetative state.

"Serious bodily injury" is a legal term meaning a substantial risk of death, serious permanent disfigurement, or protracted loss or impairment of a bodily function. Many injuries do not meet that definition. The State must also prove the intoxication caused the injury. We hire accident reconstruction experts, obtain vehicle data, and review medical records closely.

---

## Intoxication Manslaughter
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/dui-manslaughter/

Intoxication manslaughter defense in Houston and Fort Bend County: second-degree felony penalties, causation and blood evidence.

When a death results from a crash involving an intoxicated driver, the charge is intoxication manslaughter under Penal Code § 49.08, a second-degree felony punishable by two to twenty years in prison. It becomes a first-degree felony if the person who died was an on-duty peace officer, firefighter, or emergency medical worker.

These cases are emotional and heavily investigated. The strongest defenses often involve causation: whether another driver's conduct, road conditions, or the deceased person's actions actually caused the collision. We retain reconstruction and toxicology experts early. Our affiliated family firm has obtained a four-year sentence in an intoxication manslaughter case where the State sought fifteen.

---

## ALR Hearings
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/administrative-license-revocation-hearing/

How to save your driver license after a Houston DWI arrest: the 15-day ALR deadline, suspension lengths and hearing strategy.

After a DWI arrest where you refused or failed a breath or blood test, DPS will suspend your license unless you request an Administrative License Revocation hearing within 15 days of receiving notice. The hearing is held before an administrative law judge with the State Office of Administrative Hearings.

## Suspension Lengths
- Failed test, no prior alcohol contacts: 90 days.
- Refused test, no prior alcohol contacts: 180 days.
- With prior alcohol-related contacts in the past ten years: up to one year for a failure and two years for a refusal.

## Why the Hearing Matters
At the hearing, DPS must prove reasonable suspicion for the stop, probable cause for the arrest, and either a refusal or a result of 0.08 or more. We can subpoena the arresting officer and question them under oath, which often produces valuable testimony for the criminal case. If the suspension is upheld, an occupational license may let you keep driving.

---

## HPD & Fort Bend DWI Arrests
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/houston-police-department/

How DWI arrests work with the Houston Police Department, Harris County deputies, Fort Bend County Sheriff and local police.

In Houston, DWI stops are made by the Houston Police Department, including officers assigned to traffic and DWI enforcement, as well as Harris County Sheriff's deputies, constable precincts, METRO police, and DPS troopers. In Fort Bend County, they are made by the Fort Bend County Sheriff's Office, constables, Sugar Land, Missouri City, Stafford, Rosenberg and Richmond police, and DPS.

Both counties run "no refusal" enforcement, where on-call judges sign blood search warrants when a driver declines a breath test. That means blood evidence is common, and the warrant affidavit itself becomes a target for challenge. Agencies differ in equipment, video retention, and testing practices, so we request records specific to the arresting department.

After arrest, people are typically booked through the Harris County Joint Processing Center downtown or the Fort Bend County Jail in Richmond before seeing a magistrate and being released on bond.

---

## Breath Tests in DWI Cases
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/breathalyzers/

How Texas DWI breath tests work, Intoxilyzer 9000 reliability, and challenging breath results in Harris and Fort Bend Counties.

Texas uses the Intoxilyzer 9000 for evidentiary breath testing. The test requires two samples that agree within 0.02, and a certified operator must observe the subject for at least 15 minutes beforehand to make sure nothing could contaminate the result, such as burping, vomiting, or placing something in the mouth.

Portable roadside devices are a different tool and their numbers are generally not admissible to prove a specific concentration. Breath testing assumes an average relationship between breath and blood alcohol that does not fit everyone. Conditions such as acid reflux, dental work, and residual mouth alcohol can skew results.

We obtain the instrument's maintenance, inspection and calibration records, the operator's certification, and the full test record to identify problems.

---

## DWI Blood Tests
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/dwi-blood-tests/

Challenging blood test evidence in Houston DWI cases: warrants, collection, lab analysis and chain of custody.

Blood tests are often treated as the gold standard, but every step creates room for error. Since the U.S. Supreme Court's decision in Missouri v. McNeely, police generally need a warrant or valid consent to draw blood. In Harris and Fort Bend Counties, warrants are often obtained quickly from on-call judges.

## Where Blood Evidence Breaks Down
- The warrant affidavit may rely on boilerplate or inaccurate observations.
- The person drawing blood must be qualified and use proper technique.
- Tubes must contain the correct preservative and anticoagulant and be stored properly.
- Lab analysis by gas chromatography requires calibration, controls, and clean batch data.
- Chain of custody must be documented from the draw to the lab.

We request the full lab file, not just the summary report, and work with independent toxicologists when needed. You may also be entitled to have the sample retested.

---

## Field Sobriety Tests
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/field-sobriety-test/

Standardized field sobriety tests in Texas DWI cases: HGN, walk-and-turn and one-leg stand, and why officers get them wrong.

Officers are trained to administer three standardized field sobriety tests developed by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration: horizontal gaze nystagmus (HGN), the walk-and-turn, and the one-leg stand. Those tests are only considered reliable when given exactly as trained, on a suitable surface, to a person without conditions that affect balance.

Common problems include uneven or sloped roadside surfaces, flashing emergency lights during HGN, poor footwear, injuries, weight, age, nervousness, and instructions given incorrectly or too quickly. Body-camera and dash-camera footage often shows a different picture than the officer's report. You are not legally required to perform field sobriety tests in Texas.

---

## Test Refusal & Implied Consent
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/dwi-test-refusal-and-implied-consent/

Texas implied consent law: what happens if you refuse a breath or blood test after a DWI arrest in Houston or Fort Bend County.

Under Transportation Code § 724.011, anyone arrested for DWI is considered to have consented to a breath or blood test. You can still refuse, but a refusal leads to a 180-day license suspension for a first offense, can be used as evidence at trial, and often results in police seeking a blood search warrant anyway.

Officers must read the statutory warning (form DIC-24) before requesting a specimen. A refusal obtained without proper warnings, or a "consent" obtained through misleading statements, may be challenged. In certain cases, such as crashes involving serious injury or a child passenger, the law directs officers to obtain a specimen, though constitutional warrant requirements still apply.

---

## DWI Penalties in Texas
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/dwi-penalties/

Texas DWI penalties: jail ranges, fines, license suspensions, state traffic fines and ignition interlock requirements.

DWI penalties in Texas depend on prior convictions, the alcohol concentration, and whether anyone was injured or a child was in the vehicle. Beyond jail and fines, a conviction can bring:

- State traffic fine: $3,000 for a first conviction within 36 months, $4,500 for subsequent convictions, or $6,000 if the concentration was 0.16 or more.
- License suspension: 90 days to one year for a first conviction, longer for repeat offenses (often avoidable with an occupational license or interlock).
- Ignition interlock: required in many repeat and high-BAC cases.
- Classes and community service: DWI education, a victim impact panel, and community service hours.
- Insurance: SR-22 filing and higher premiums.

---

## The Cost of a DWI
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/cost-of-a-dwi/

What a DWI really costs in Houston: bond, fines, state traffic fines, interlock, insurance and legal fees.

The financial impact of a DWI reaches far beyond the court fine. Typical costs include bond, towing and impound fees, fines and court costs, the state traffic fine of $3,000 to $6,000 after conviction, ignition interlock installation and monthly monitoring, DWI education classes, higher insurance premiums with an SR-22 filing, and time away from work for court settings.

A conviction can also affect employment, professional licenses, and travel. That is why a strong defense often costs less in the long run than a quick plea. We quote a flat fee for most DWI cases after a free consultation, so you know your legal cost from the start.

---

## The DWI Process
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/dwi-process/

Step-by-step guide to the DWI process in Harris and Fort Bend County, from arrest and bond to trial.

1. Stop and investigation: The officer observes driving, makes contact, and may request field sobriety tests.
2. Arrest and testing: You are asked for a breath or blood specimen, or a warrant is sought.
3. Booking and magistration: A magistrate sets bond and conditions, which may include an interlock or alcohol monitoring.
4. ALR deadline: You have 15 days to request an ALR hearing.
5. First court setting: The case is filed in a county court at law (misdemeanor) or district court (felony).
6. Discovery and investigation: We obtain video, reports, and test records under Article 39.14.
7. Motions: Suppression motions can eliminate evidence obtained unlawfully.
8. Resolution or trial: Dismissal, reduction, a negotiated outcome, or a jury or bench trial.

---

## Misdemeanor DWI Process
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/misdemeanor-dwi-process/

How a misdemeanor DWI moves through the Harris County and Fort Bend County court-at-law system.

Misdemeanor DWIs in Harris County are heard in the county criminal courts at law at the Criminal Justice Center downtown. In Fort Bend County, they are heard in the county courts at law at the Justice Center in Richmond. Cases typically take several months, with multiple settings while discovery is exchanged and lab results are completed.

Bond conditions can include reporting, no alcohol, and an interlock. We often handle routine settings without the client needing to miss work, though you must appear when the court requires. Throughout the case we evaluate suppression motions, diversion eligibility, and whether a trial gives you the best result.

---

## DWI Reduction & Dismissal
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/dwi-reduction-and-dismissal/

How DWI charges get reduced or dismissed in Houston and Fort Bend County.

DWI cases are dismissed or reduced when the evidence does not hold up. Common reasons include an unlawful stop, an arrest without probable cause, field sobriety tests that were improperly given, breath-test procedure failures, blood-draw or lab problems, and video that contradicts the report.

Reductions may include obstructing a highway, reckless driving, or other non-DWI offenses that avoid the state traffic fine, the DWI label, and enhancement for future cases. Each prosecutor's office has its own policies, so knowing the local practices in Harris and Fort Bend Counties matters.

---

## DWI Deferred Adjudication
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/dwi-deferred-adjudication/

Deferred adjudication for DWI in Texas: eligibility, interlock requirements and nondisclosure.

Since September 1, 2019, judges may grant deferred adjudication in many DWI cases. With deferred, there is no conviction if you complete the terms, and the case is dismissed.

Deferred is not available to people who held a commercial driver's license at the time of the offense or who had an alcohol concentration of 0.15 or more. The court must require an ignition interlock as a condition. A deferred DWI still counts as a prior if you are arrested again, and it may qualify for an order of nondisclosure after a waiting period.

---

## DWI Pretrial Diversion
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/dwi-pre-trial-diversion-program/

DWI pretrial diversion and intervention programs in Harris and Fort Bend Counties: eligibility and benefits.

Pretrial diversion, sometimes called pretrial intervention, is an agreement with the prosecutor that pauses the case while you complete conditions such as classes, community service, and monitoring. If you complete the program, the case is dismissed and may be eligible for expunction.

Eligibility and availability for DWI cases vary by county and change with prosecutor policy. Generally, first-time arrests without an accident, a high BAC, or aggravating factors are the strongest candidates. We assess whether you qualify and advocate for admission.

---

## DWI Probation
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/dwi-probation/

What DWI probation (community supervision) looks like in Harris and Fort Bend County.

Community supervision lets you serve a sentence in the community instead of jail. For a misdemeanor DWI, probation may last up to two years. Common conditions include reporting to a probation officer, fees, a DWI education program, a victim impact panel, community service, alcohol evaluation and treatment, and in many cases an ignition interlock.

Violations can lead to a motion to revoke and jail time. If you are struggling with conditions, contact us early. Courts are often willing to modify terms when a lawyer explains the situation before a violation is filed.

---

## DWI Specialty Courts
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/dwi-court-program/

DWI and sobriety specialty court programs in Harris and Fort Bend Counties for eligible repeat offenders.

Harris and Fort Bend Counties operate specialty treatment courts designed for people whose cases are connected to substance use. These programs combine intensive supervision, treatment, frequent testing, and regular appearances before a judge.

For eligible clients, especially those facing a repeat DWI, a specialty court can offer a path that avoids long jail or prison sentences and addresses the underlying issue. Programs are demanding, so we discuss whether one fits your circumstances before you apply.

---

## Occupational Driver License
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/occupational-drivers-license/

How to get an occupational driver license in Texas after a DWI suspension in Houston or Fort Bend County.

An occupational driver license (sometimes called an essential need license) lets you drive during a suspension for work, school, and household duties. It is obtained by filing a petition in court and then submitting the order to DPS with proof of SR-22 insurance.

Orders typically limit driving to certain hours and purposes and may require an ignition interlock. When an interlock is ordered, many time-of-day restrictions do not apply, and in many cases the usual waiting period can be avoided. We prepare and file petitions as part of our DWI representation.

---

## Ignition Interlock Devices
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/ignition-interlock-devices/

When Texas courts require an ignition interlock after a DWI and how to comply.

An ignition interlock is a breath-testing device installed in your vehicle that prevents it from starting if it detects alcohol, and that requires periodic retests while driving. Texas law requires an interlock as a bond condition for repeat DWI and intoxication assault or manslaughter charges, as a condition of DWI deferred adjudication, and for probation in high-BAC cases. Judges may order one in other cases too.

Violations, including missed retests or readings from mouthwash or food, are reported to the court. We help clients understand the reporting rules and respond quickly when a reading is disputed.

---

## SCRAM & Alcohol Monitoring
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/scram-and-alcohol-monitoring/

SCRAM ankle monitors and portable alcohol monitors as DWI bond and probation conditions in Houston.

Courts may order continuous alcohol monitoring through a transdermal ankle device, or a portable breath device that requires tests at scheduled times. These conditions are common in repeat DWI cases and when a high BAC is alleged.

Monitoring can be costly and invasive. After a period of compliance, we can ask the court to remove or reduce monitoring conditions. When a reading is alleged, we review the raw data, because environmental alcohol and device errors can produce false alerts.

---

## DWI Terms Glossary
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/dwi-terms/

Glossary of common Texas DWI terms: BAC, ALR, SFST, HGN, DIC-24, interlock, nondisclosure and more.

- BAC: Blood or breath alcohol concentration. The per se limit is 0.08.
- ALR: Administrative License Revocation, the DPS license suspension process.
- DIC-24: The statutory warning read before requesting a breath or blood specimen.
- SFSTs: Standardized field sobriety tests: HGN, walk-and-turn and one-leg stand.
- HGN: Horizontal gaze nystagmus, an involuntary jerking of the eyes.
- Loss of normal use: The non-numeric definition of intoxication.
- Interlock: A breath device that prevents a vehicle from starting after alcohol consumption.
- Occupational license: A restricted license to drive during a suspension.
- Deferred adjudication: Supervision without a conviction if completed.
- Nondisclosure: An order sealing certain records from public view.
- Retrograde extrapolation: Estimating BAC at the time of driving from a later test.

---

## DWI FAQ
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/dwi-faq/

Answers to frequently asked questions about DWI arrests in Houston and Fort Bend County.

Here are answers to questions DWI clients in Houston, Sugar Land, Richmond and Katy ask most often.

Q: Will I lose my license after a DWI arrest?
A: Possibly, unless you request an ALR hearing within 15 days. Even if a suspension is upheld, you may qualify for an occupational license.

Q: Can I get a DWI if I was under 0.08?
A: Yes. Texas also defines intoxication as losing the normal use of your mental or physical faculties, so a DWI can be charged below 0.08.

Q: Should I have refused the breath test?
A: A refusal carries a longer license suspension and can be used as evidence, but it may also limit the State's scientific evidence. Every case is different; what matters now is reviewing what actually happened.

Q: Is jail mandatory for a first DWI?
A: The law sets a 72-hour minimum if jail is imposed, but many first-time clients receive probation, deferred adjudication, or a reduction instead.

Q: Can a DWI be expunged?
A: Only if the case is dismissed, no-billed or results in acquittal. A first DWI that ends in conviction or deferred may qualify for nondisclosure instead.

---

## DWI and Carrying a Weapon
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/dwi-and-unlawful-possession-of-a-weapon/

DWI arrests involving a handgun in Texas: unlawful carrying charges and License to Carry consequences.

Texas permits most adults 21 and older to carry a handgun without a license, but carrying a handgun in a vehicle while committing another offense, such as DWI, can result in a separate Class A charge for unlawfully carrying a weapon. License to Carry holders who carry while intoxicated face their own Class A offense and possible suspension or revocation of the license.

When a weapon is involved, prosecutors often treat the DWI more seriously. Defeating or reducing the DWI can also defeat the weapons charge, so we defend the two together.

---

## Drug-Related DWI
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/drug-related-dwi/

DWI charges based on prescription drugs, marijuana or other substances in Houston and Fort Bend County.

A DWI does not require alcohol. Texas law covers intoxication by any controlled substance, drug, dangerous drug, or combination. Unlike alcohol, there is no per se legal limit for most drugs, so the State must prove you lost the normal use of your faculties.

Drug-DWI cases often rely on a Drug Recognition Expert evaluation and a blood test. Blood results can show a substance was present without showing impairment at the time of driving. We challenge the DRE protocol, the lab's methods, and the link between the substance and the driving.

---

## Marijuana DWI
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/marijuana-dwi/

Defending DWI charges based on marijuana or THC in Houston and Fort Bend County.

THC can remain in blood long after any impairment has worn off, especially in regular users. Because Texas has no per se THC limit for driving, the State must prove marijuana actually caused a loss of normal use. Field sobriety tests designed for alcohol are not validated for marijuana impairment.

Hemp-derived products, which are legal in Texas when they meet the THC limits, add another layer: lab reports may not distinguish legal from illegal sources. We examine the officer's observations, any DRE evaluation, and the toxicology carefully.

---

## Prescription Drug DWI
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/prescription-dwi/

DWI charges involving lawfully prescribed medication in Texas and how to defend them.

Having a valid prescription is not a defense to DWI by itself, but it often explains behavior officers misread as impairment. Many medications, including sleep aids, anxiety medications, and pain relievers, are taken safely at therapeutic doses.

We gather the prescription history, physician input, and pharmacology expertise to show whether the level detected was consistent with normal use and whether it plausibly caused impairment. Medical conditions such as diabetes, neurological issues, and fatigue can also mimic intoxication.

---

## Under-the-Limit DWI
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/under-the-limit-dwi/

Can you be charged with DWI under 0.08 in Texas? How loss-of-normal-use cases are defended.

Yes. When a breath or blood result comes back below 0.08, prosecutors may still proceed on the theory that you lost the normal use of your mental or physical faculties. These cases rely almost entirely on the officer's observations and video.

That makes them very defensible. A low test result is strong evidence in your favor, and video often shows clear speech and steady movement that contradict the report. We use the officer's own training standards to expose subjective conclusions.

---

## Auto-Brewery Syndrome
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/auto-brewery-syndrome-in-texas-dwi-cases/

Auto-brewery syndrome as a defense in Texas DWI cases: what it is and how it is proven.

Auto-brewery syndrome is a rare medical condition in which yeast in the digestive tract ferments carbohydrates into alcohol, raising a person's alcohol level without drinking. It has been documented in medical literature and raised in DWI cases.

The defense requires credible medical evidence, usually testing and diagnosis by a physician, along with toxicology that fits the explanation. We evaluate whether the facts support it and work with medical experts when they do. Other conditions, including GERD and diabetes, can also affect breath testing.

---

## DWI With an Accident or Property Damage
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/dwi-with-property-damage/

DWI arrests after a crash in Houston: property damage, restitution and enhanced investigation.

A crash does not change the basic DWI offense level when no one is seriously hurt, but it changes how the case is investigated and negotiated. Officers often arrive after the fact, so they did not see the driving, and injuries from the collision can mimic signs of intoxication. Airbag deployment, shock, and head injuries affect field sobriety testing.

Prosecutors may seek restitution for damage and may be less willing to offer diversion. We review crash reports, scene photos, vehicle data, and timing to test whether the State can prove you were intoxicated when you were driving.

---

## Obstruction of a Highway
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/obstruction-of-a-highway/

Obstructing a highway as a reduced charge in Texas DWI cases.

Obstructing a highway or other passageway under Penal Code § 42.03 is a Class B misdemeanor that is sometimes negotiated in place of a DWI. Although the offense level matches a first DWI, it avoids the DWI label, the state traffic fine, automatic license consequences, and use as a DWI enhancement in the future.

Whether this reduction is realistic depends on the evidence and the prosecutor's policies. A strong defense investigation is what creates the leverage to obtain it.

---

## Commercial Driver DWI
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/commercial-dwi/

DWI charges for CDL holders in Texas: 0.04 limits, disqualification and protecting your livelihood.

Commercial drivers face stricter rules. The alcohol limit while operating a commercial motor vehicle is 0.04. A DWI conviction or a test refusal, even in a personal vehicle, can disqualify a CDL holder for one year (three years if transporting hazardous materials), and a second offense can lead to lifetime disqualification.

CDL holders are also not eligible for DWI deferred adjudication and cannot obtain an occupational license to drive a commercial vehicle. Because the stakes are a career, we fight both the ALR suspension and the criminal case aggressively.

---

## Boating While Intoxicated
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/bwi/

Boating while intoxicated charges on Lake Houston, Galveston Bay and other Texas waters.

Boating while intoxicated under Penal Code § 49.06 applies to operating a watercraft while intoxicated. It is a Class B misdemeanor for a first offense and is enhanced like DWI with prior convictions. Texas Parks and Wildlife game wardens and local marine units patrol Lake Houston, Lake Conroe, Clear Lake, and Galveston Bay.

Sun, wind, wave motion, and fatigue all affect balance and appearance on the water, which makes standard field sobriety tests unreliable. Officers sometimes use seated tests that are not standardized. We challenge the stop, the testing, and whether the person was actually operating the vessel.

---

## Flying While Intoxicated
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/flying-while-intoxicated/

Flying while intoxicated charges in Texas and FAA consequences for pilots.

Operating an aircraft while intoxicated is an offense under Penal Code § 49.05, a Class B misdemeanor for a first offense. Federal rules separately prohibit acting as a crew member within eight hours of drinking or with a concentration of 0.04 or more.

Pilots also face FAA reporting obligations and certificate actions, so the criminal and regulatory issues must be handled together. See our page on pilot license consequences.

---

## Underage DWI
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/underage-dwi/

DUI and DWI charges for drivers under 21 in Texas: zero tolerance, license suspension and record protection.

Texas has a zero-tolerance policy for drivers under 21. A minor who operates a vehicle with any detectable amount of alcohol can be charged with Driving Under the Influence by a Minor (DUI) under the Alcoholic Beverage Code, a Class C offense that still carries a license suspension, alcohol education, and community service.

If the State believes the minor was intoxicated, it may instead file a DWI, which carries adult penalties. A first DUI by a minor may be expunged if certain conditions are met. Early defense protects school, scholarships and future employment.

---

## Student DWI
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/student-dwi/

DWI defense for college students at UH, TSU, Rice, HCC and other Houston-area schools.

A DWI arrest can affect enrollment, scholarships, campus housing, study-abroad plans, and professional school applications. Students at the University of Houston, Texas Southern University, Rice University, Houston Community College, and other schools may also face campus discipline.

We work toward outcomes that keep a conviction off the record, such as dismissal, diversion, or a reduction, and we advise on how to answer application questions about arrests honestly and accurately.

---

## Defending Women Charged With DWI
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/defending-women/

DWI defense considerations for women in Houston and Fort Bend County.

Women charged with DWI face the same law, but some practical factors deserve attention. Footwear such as heels or sandals can affect walk-and-turn and one-leg-stand performance, and many officers do not offer an alternative. Medications, hormonal changes and medical conditions can influence how alcohol is absorbed and how breath tests read.

Many of our clients are also balancing careers and caregiving. We focus on resolutions that protect licenses, employment, and family responsibilities, and we handle routine settings to reduce time away from home.

---

## Expunging DWI Records
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/expunging-dwi-records/

When a Texas DWI arrest can be expunged and how the process works in Harris and Fort Bend County.

An expunction erases the arrest record and allows you to deny it in most situations. A DWI arrest can be expunged if the case was dismissed (subject to certain conditions and waiting periods), no-billed by a grand jury, or ended in acquittal, or after completing a pretrial diversion program.

A DWI that ended in conviction or deferred adjudication cannot be expunged, but may qualify for nondisclosure. See Sealing DWI Records and Expunctions & Record Sealing.

---

## Sealing DWI Records
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/sealing-dwi-records/

Orders of nondisclosure for first-time DWI convictions and deferred adjudication in Texas.

Texas allows certain first-time DWI offenders to seal their records with an order of nondisclosure. Generally, the offense must have been a first DWI with a concentration below 0.15, without an accident involving another person, and the person must have completed their sentence and the required waiting period. The waiting period is shorter if an ignition interlock was used for at least six months.

A nondisclosure order prevents most private employers and landlords from seeing the record through public databases, although law enforcement and certain licensing agencies can still access it.

---

## DWI & Professional Licenses
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/professional-licenses/

How a DWI affects nurses, doctors, teachers, pilots and military members in Texas.

For licensed professionals, the consequences of a DWI can be more serious than the court sentence. Many licensing boards require self-reporting, review arrests as well as convictions, and evaluate substance-use concerns.

We coordinate the criminal defense with licensing strategy so that the outcome of the case, and how it is described to your board, protects your career. See the pages below for specific professions.

---

## DWI and Nursing Licenses
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/professional-licenses/nursing-license-revocation/

How a DWI affects Texas nursing licenses and Board of Nursing reporting.

The Texas Board of Nursing considers criminal history in licensing and renewal and asks nurses about arrests and convictions. Alcohol-related offenses can lead to board inquiries, peer assistance referrals, or conditions on a license.

Answering board questions accurately is critical; incomplete answers can create more trouble than the underlying case. We pursue outcomes, such as dismissal or diversion, that minimize what must be reported.

---

## DWI and Medical Licenses
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/professional-licenses/medical-license-revocation/

DWI consequences for physicians and Texas Medical Board licensure.

Physicians licensed by the Texas Medical Board may face questions about alcohol-related arrests at renewal and in hospital credentialing. A pattern of alcohol offenses can prompt evaluation or monitoring through physician health programs.

We work to resolve the criminal case in a way that limits professional fallout and advise on accurate disclosures to the board and employers.

---

## DWI and Teaching Certificates
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/professional-licenses/teaching-certification-revocation/

How DWI arrests affect Texas educator certification and school employment.

Texas educators are subject to criminal history review by the State Board for Educator Certification and their districts. Districts in Houston ISD, Fort Bend ISD, Katy ISD and elsewhere may receive notice of arrests through fingerprint-based monitoring.

An alcohol offense on its own does not always threaten certification, but how the case is resolved and reported matters. We focus on outcomes that keep your record and career intact.

---

## DWI and Pilot Certificates
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/professional-licenses/pilot-license-revocation/

FAA reporting requirements for pilots after a DWI arrest or license suspension.

Pilots must report alcohol-related motor vehicle actions, including DWI convictions and administrative license suspensions, to the FAA's Security and Investigations Division within 60 days. Medical certificate applications also ask about these events.

Failing to report can itself lead to certificate action. We help pilots meet reporting deadlines while defending the criminal case and the ALR suspension.

---

## Military Members Charged With DWI
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/dwi-dui/professional-licenses/active-military-members-charged-with-dwi/

DWI defense for active-duty service members and veterans in Houston and Fort Bend County.

Service members arrested off base are prosecuted in civilian court, but a DWI may also be reported to the command and affect security clearances, promotions, and base driving privileges. Veterans may be eligible for veterans treatment court programs in Harris or Fort Bend County.

We coordinate with clients on command reporting and pursue resolutions that limit both civilian and military consequences.

## Houston & Fort Bend County Drug Crime Lawyer
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/drug-charges/

Houston and Fort Bend County drug crime lawyer: possession, delivery, trafficking, fentanyl, cocaine, meth and prescription drug charges. Call (832) 979-0882.

Texas prosecutes drug offenses under the Health and Safety Code, which sorts substances into penalty groups. The penalty depends on the group, the weight (including adulterants and dilutants), and whether the State alleges simple possession or intent to deliver. A small difference in weight can move a case from a state jail felony to a first-degree felony.

## Common Drug Charges in Houston
We defend possession of cocaine, methamphetamine, heroin, fentanyl, ecstasy, prescription pills and THC concentrates, as well as possession with intent to deliver, manufacture, trafficking and prescription fraud. Many cases arise from traffic stops on I-45, I-10, US-59/I-69 and Highway 6, from searches of apartments and vehicles, and from investigations by HPD's narcotics units, county task forces, and federal agencies.

## Programs That Can Protect Your Record
Harris and Fort Bend Counties offer pretrial intervention and specialty drug courts for eligible clients. Successful completion can lead to dismissal and, in many cases, expunction. Early representation improves the chance of being accepted.

---

## Texas Drug Penalty Groups
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/drug-charges/texas-penalty-groups/

How Texas drug penalty groups work: which drugs fall in Penalty Groups 1, 1-A, 1-B, 2, 2-A, 3 and 4.

Texas classifies controlled substances into penalty groups in Chapter 481 of the Health and Safety Code.

- Penalty Group 1: cocaine, methamphetamine, heroin, oxycodone, hydrocodone and other opioids.
- Penalty Group 1-A: LSD, measured in dosage units.
- Penalty Group 1-B: fentanyl and its analogues, created in 2023 with harsher delivery penalties.
- Penalty Group 2: ecstasy (MDMA), PCP, psilocybin mushrooms, amphetamine and THC concentrates such as vape oil and wax.
- Penalty Group 2-A: synthetic cannabinoids (K2, spice).
- Penalty Group 3: benzodiazepines such as Xanax and Valium, and certain other prescription drugs.
- Penalty Group 4: small amounts of certain opiates in compounds, such as some codeine cough syrups.

Marijuana is treated separately by weight. Knowing exactly which group the State alleges, and whether the lab confirmed it, is the first step in any drug defense.

---

## Possession of a Controlled Substance
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/drug-charges/possession-of-a-controlled-substance/

Possession of a controlled substance charges in Houston and Fort Bend County: penalty groups, weights and defenses.

Possession of a controlled substance means knowingly exercising care, custody, control or management over a drug listed in the Health and Safety Code. When drugs are found in a shared car or home, the State must show "affirmative links" connecting you to them, such as ownership, proximity, conduct, or statements. Presence alone is not enough.

The punishment depends on the penalty group and the aggregate weight, which includes any cutting agents. The table below shows the ranges for Penalty Group 1, the most common group in Houston felony drug cases.

---

## State Jail Felony Drug Charges
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/drug-charges/state-jail-felony-drug-charges/

State jail felony drug possession in Texas: less than one gram, mandatory probation and diversion options.

Possessing less than one gram of a Penalty Group 1 drug, such as cocaine or methamphetamine, is a state jail felony. These "under a gram" cases make up a large share of felony dockets in Harris County.

For many first-time defendants, Texas law requires that the sentence be probated rather than served in a state jail. Some cases can be reduced to a Class A misdemeanor under Penal Code § 12.44. Pretrial intervention and drug court may lead to dismissal. Lab weight and trace-amount issues are also important: very small residue may not support prosecution at all.

---

## Possession of Cocaine
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/drug-charges/possession-of-cocaine/

Cocaine possession charges in Houston and Fort Bend County: Penalty Group 1 weights, penalties and defenses.

Cocaine, including crack cocaine, is a Penalty Group 1 controlled substance. Possession of less than a gram is a state jail felony; larger amounts quickly become second- or first-degree felonies.

Common defenses include challenging the traffic stop or search, disputing knowing possession when the drugs were found in a shared space, and testing the lab's identification and weight. Residue in a pipe or baggie may be too small to test or prosecute.

---

## Possession of Methamphetamine
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/drug-charges/possession-of-methamphetamine/

Methamphetamine possession charges in Harris and Fort Bend County: penalties and defenses.

Methamphetamine is a Penalty Group 1 drug. Because meth is often sold mixed with other substances, the aggregate weight used by the lab, which includes those mixtures, can push a charge into a higher category.

We examine the search, the chain of custody, and the lab's methods for weighing and identifying the substance. Clients struggling with addiction may qualify for drug court, which combines treatment with the chance of a dismissal.

---

## Possession of Heroin
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/drug-charges/possession-of-heroin/

Heroin possession charges in Houston and Fort Bend County: penalties and treatment-based alternatives.

Heroin is a Penalty Group 1 controlled substance, carrying the same weight-based ranges as cocaine and methamphetamine. Heroin is also increasingly mixed with fentanyl, which can raise the stakes in delivery cases.

In addition to search and possession defenses, we explore treatment-based resolutions where appropriate. Texas's Good Samaritan law offers a limited defense to possession for someone who calls 911 for an overdose, subject to conditions.

---

## Possession of Fentanyl
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/drug-charges/possession-of-fentanyl/

Fentanyl charges in Texas: Penalty Group 1-B, enhanced delivery penalties, and fentanyl-related murder charges.

In 2023, Texas moved fentanyl into its own Penalty Group 1-B and raised penalties for manufacturing and delivery. Possession of even small amounts is a felony. If fentanyl delivered by someone causes a death, prosecutors can now charge murder.

Many people charged with fentanyl offenses believed they had a different drug, such as a counterfeit pill sold as a prescription medication. Knowledge, identification, and causation are central issues. We retain toxicology and pharmacology experts when the facts require it.

---

## Opioid Possession
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/drug-charges/opioid-possession/

Defending possession of oxycodone, hydrocodone and other opioid charges in Houston.

Most prescription opioids, including oxycodone and hydrocodone, are Penalty Group 1 drugs, so possession without a valid prescription is charged the same way as cocaine or heroin. Pills are weighed in full, not by the amount of active ingredient, which can inflate the weight.

A valid prescription is a defense to possession of your own medication. We also examine whether pills were properly identified by laboratory testing rather than markings alone.

---

## Possession of Xanax
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/drug-charges/possession-of-xanax/

Possession of Xanax (alprazolam) charges in Texas: Penalty Group 3 penalties and defenses.

Alprazolam, sold as Xanax, is a Penalty Group 3 substance. Possession of less than 28 grams, which includes the full weight of the pills, is a Class A misdemeanor. Larger amounts are felonies.

Counterfeit "Xanax" pills sometimes contain fentanyl or other substances, which can change the charge entirely. We review the lab results carefully and raise prescription and knowledge defenses where they apply.

---

## Possession of Adderall
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/drug-charges/possession-of-adderall/

Possession of Adderall without a prescription in Houston and Fort Bend County: penalties and defenses.

Adderall contains amphetamine, which Texas classifies in Penalty Group 2. Possession of less than one gram, including the full pill weight, can be a state jail felony, and a handful of pills can exceed that threshold.

These cases often involve students and young professionals who never thought of a borrowed pill as a felony. Diversion programs are frequently available, and a valid prescription is a defense.

---

## Possession of Ecstasy
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/drug-charges/possession-of-ecstasy/

Ecstasy and MDMA possession charges in Texas: Penalty Group 2 penalties and defenses.

MDMA, commonly called ecstasy or molly, is a Penalty Group 2 controlled substance. Possession of less than one gram is a state jail felony, and amounts from four to 400 grams are a second-degree felony.

Pills and powders sold as MDMA often contain other drugs. The State must prove what the substance actually was through laboratory testing. Arrests at concerts and festivals also raise questions about search procedures and consent.

---

## Possession of Psilocybin Mushrooms
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/drug-charges/possession-of-mushrooms/

Psilocybin mushroom possession charges in Texas: weight issues and penalties.

Psilocybin and psilocin are Penalty Group 2 substances in Texas. Because the State often weighs the entire mushroom rather than the active compound, a modest amount of dried mushrooms can reach serious felony weight ranges.

Weight methodology is a key issue in these cases. We also challenge searches and knowledge, particularly with edibles or products whose contents were not clear.

---

## Possession of Synthetic Marijuana
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/drug-charges/possession-of-synthetic-marijuana/

Synthetic marijuana (K2, spice) possession charges in Texas: Penalty Group 2-A.

Synthetic cannabinoids, often sold as K2 or spice, are in Penalty Group 2-A, which is punished by weight similar to marijuana: two ounces or less is a Class B misdemeanor, and larger quantities climb to felony levels.

Chemical formulas for these products change frequently, so the lab must confirm the specific compound is listed in the statute.

---

## Possession of a Dangerous Drug
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/drug-charges/possession-of-a-dangerous-drug/

Possession of a dangerous drug without a prescription in Texas: Class A misdemeanor charges and defenses.

"Dangerous drugs" are prescription medications that are not controlled substances, such as certain muscle relaxers, antidepressants, and testosterone in some forms. Possessing one without a valid prescription is generally a Class A misdemeanor under Health and Safety Code Chapter 483.

A prescription in your name, or a lawful reason for possession, is a defense. These cases are often good candidates for dismissal or diversion.

---

## Possession of Drug Paraphernalia
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/drug-charges/possession-of-drug-paraphernalia/

Drug paraphernalia charges in Houston: Class C possession, Class A delivery, and keeping a clean record.

Possession of drug paraphernalia, such as pipes, scales, or baggies intended for use with drugs, is a Class C misdemeanor punishable by a fine only. Delivering or selling paraphernalia is a Class A misdemeanor.

Even a Class C conviction creates a criminal record. Deferred disposition often allows the case to be dismissed and later expunged.

---

## Drug-Free Zone Enhancements
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/drug-charges/possession-in-a-drug-free-zone/

Drug-free zone enhancements in Texas: schools, youth centers and playgrounds.

Texas increases punishment for certain drug offenses committed within 1,000 feet of a school, or within 300 feet of a youth center, public pool, or video arcade, and on school buses. Depending on the offense, the enhancement can raise the offense level, increase minimum sentences, or double fines.

The State must prove the location and distance with competent evidence, and the enhancement must be properly pleaded. We frequently find measurement and mapping errors.

---

## Possession With Intent to Deliver
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/drug-charges/possession-with-intent-to-distribute/

Possession with intent to deliver charges in Harris and Fort Bend County: what the State must prove.

Texas charges possession with intent to deliver under the same statute as manufacture and delivery, with higher penalties than simple possession. Prosecutors usually try to prove intent through quantity, packaging, scales, cash, or text messages rather than any observed sale.

Each of those factors has innocent explanations. We challenge the inference of intent and push to reduce the charge to simple possession, which can make a significant difference in exposure.

---

## Drug Trafficking
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/drug-charges/drug-trafficking/

Drug trafficking and delivery defense in Houston: state and federal charges along the I-10 and US-59 corridors.

Houston's highways and port make it a focus of state and federal trafficking investigations. Large-quantity cases may be charged in state court as manufacture or delivery, or federally under 21 U.S.C. § 841 with mandatory minimum sentences.

These investigations often rely on wiretaps, confidential informants, controlled buys and vehicle searches. We challenge the legality of each technique, the credibility of informants, and the government's proof of knowledge, and we evaluate federal safety-valve and cooperation issues where relevant. See Federal Crimes.

---

## Prescription Drug Fraud
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/drug-charges/prescription-drug-fraud/

Prescription fraud charges in Texas: forged prescriptions, doctor shopping and pharmacy cases.

Obtaining a controlled substance by fraud, such as through a forged or altered prescription or misrepresentation to a doctor or pharmacy, is a felony in Texas. The level depends on the penalty group of the drug involved.

These cases are document-heavy and often involve pharmacy records and surveillance video. We examine whether the State can prove you knew the prescription was invalid and whether identification is reliable.

---

## Diversion of Controlled Substances
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/drug-charges/diversion-of-controlled-substance/

Diversion of controlled substances by healthcare professionals in Texas: criminal and licensing exposure.

Physicians, nurses, pharmacists, and other registrants can be charged when controlled substances are diverted from lawful medical use. These cases often arise from audits, DEA or state board investigations, or pharmacy inventory discrepancies.

Because licensing and criminal exposure overlap, we coordinate the defense with your professional obligations and engage with investigators early, before charges are filed when possible.

---

## Houston & Fort Bend Marijuana Defense Lawyer
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/marijuana-defense/

Houston and Fort Bend County marijuana defense lawyer: possession, THC vape and wax, distribution and cultivation charges.

Marijuana remains illegal in Texas outside of the limited Compassionate Use Program, but enforcement varies widely between counties. Harris County has offered a misdemeanor marijuana diversion program for years, while practices in Fort Bend County and surrounding areas have changed over time.

The 2019 legalization of hemp with low delta-9 THC has made marijuana prosecutions more complicated, because the State must prove the THC concentration through laboratory testing. Odor or appearance alone may not distinguish legal hemp from illegal marijuana.

THC concentrates, including vape cartridges, wax, and edibles, are treated far more harshly than plant marijuana because they fall in Penalty Group 2. A single vape pen can be a felony.

---

## Possession of Marijuana
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/marijuana-defense/possession-of-marijuana/

Marijuana possession charges in Harris and Fort Bend County: penalties, diversion and defenses.

Possession of two ounces or less of marijuana is a Class B misdemeanor in Texas, but the penalties grow with weight. Usable marijuana is weighed, not stems or seeds where the lab properly separates them.

In Harris County, eligible people may be offered a diversion program that avoids a conviction. Even where diversion is not offered, we often obtain dismissals by challenging the search, the lab's ability to distinguish hemp, and whether the State can link the marijuana to you.

---

## Possession of THC Oil, Vapes & Edibles
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/marijuana-defense/possession-of-thc-oil/

THC vape, wax and edible charges in Texas: Penalty Group 2 felony exposure and defenses.

Texas classifies THC concentrates, including vape oil, wax, shatter, and many edibles, as Penalty Group 2 substances. Possession of less than one gram is a state jail felony, and because the entire weight of an edible or cartridge contents may be counted, charges can quickly escalate.

Laws governing hemp-derived THC products have been the subject of ongoing legislation and litigation. Many products sold in stores are labeled as hemp. The State must prove the product exceeded the legal delta-9 THC limit through valid testing, and must prove you knew what you possessed.

---

## Cite and Release for Marijuana
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/marijuana-defense/cite-and-release/

Cite-and-release and marijuana diversion programs in Houston and Fort Bend County.

Texas law allows officers to issue a citation instead of making an arrest for certain misdemeanors, including possession of up to four ounces of marijuana, if the county has adopted a policy. A citation still requires you to appear in court and still results in a criminal charge.

Harris County has used a pre-charge diversion approach for small marijuana cases, under which eligible people complete a class instead of being charged. Policies change, so we confirm current options in the county where your case is pending.

---

## Marijuana Distribution
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/marijuana-defense/marijuana-distribution/

Delivery and distribution of marijuana charges in Texas: penalties and defenses.

Delivery of marijuana ranges from a Class B misdemeanor for giving away a quarter ounce or less to a first-degree felony for large quantities. Offering to sell also counts as delivery under Texas law.

Distribution cases often rely on informants, undercover purchases, or text messages. We challenge identification, entrapment and the reliability of the evidence used to prove intent.

---

## Marijuana Cultivation & Grow Houses
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/marijuana-defense/marijuana-cultivation-and-growhouses/

Marijuana cultivation and grow house charges in Houston: weight calculations, searches and defenses.

Texas generally prosecutes cultivation as possession, based on the weight of the usable marijuana. Grow-house cases often begin with utility records, thermal observations, informant tips, or odor, and usually involve a search warrant.

We scrutinize the probable cause behind the warrant, the way plants were weighed, and whether occupants of a shared property actually knew about or controlled the grow.

---

## Houston & Fort Bend Violent Crimes Lawyer
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/violent-crimes/

Houston and Fort Bend County violent crime defense lawyer: assault, aggravated assault, robbery, murder, kidnapping and terroristic threat charges.

Violent-crime charges carry the most serious consequences in Texas law, and many come with a "deadly weapon" finding that limits probation and parole. These cases also tend to move fast, with high bonds and protective conditions set at the first appearance.

Our family of firms has secured dismissals in aggravated assault with a deadly weapon cases, no-bills in murder investigations, and the dismissal of a capital murder charge. We investigate independently, interview witnesses before memories fade, collect surveillance video before it is overwritten, and evaluate self-defense from day one.

## Self-Defense in Texas
Texas law justifies force when a person reasonably believes it is immediately necessary to protect against another's unlawful force, and deadly force in narrower circumstances, including to prevent certain violent felonies. In many situations there is no duty to retreat. When the evidence raises self-defense, the State must disprove it beyond a reasonable doubt.

---

## Assault by Contact
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/violent-crimes/assault-by-contact/

Class C assault by contact charges in Houston and Fort Bend County and how to keep them off your record.

Assault by offensive or provocative contact is the least serious form of assault in Texas: intentionally or knowingly causing physical contact that the person knows the other will regard as offensive. It is usually a Class C misdemeanor punishable by a fine, but it becomes a Class A misdemeanor if the victim is elderly or disabled.

Even a fine-only offense can appear on background checks and, when it involves a family member, can lead to an affirmative finding of family violence. We pursue dismissal or deferred disposition so the record can later be expunged.

---

## Assault Causing Bodily Injury
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/violent-crimes/assault-causing-bodily-injury/

Assault causing bodily injury charges in Harris and Fort Bend County: Class A penalties and enhancements.

Assault causing bodily injury under Penal Code § 22.01(a)(1) means intentionally, knowingly, or recklessly causing bodily injury, which Texas defines broadly as physical pain, illness, or any impairment of physical condition. It is typically a Class A misdemeanor.

The charge becomes a third-degree felony when the complainant is a public servant, a security officer, emergency services personnel, or a family or household member in certain circumstances, such as a prior family violence conviction or impeding breath. Self-defense, mutual combat, and lack of injury are common defenses.

---

## Aggravated Assault
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/violent-crimes/assault-with-serious-bodily-injury/

Aggravated assault charges in Houston and Fort Bend County: serious bodily injury, deadly weapons and defenses.

Aggravated assault under Penal Code § 22.02 is an assault that causes serious bodily injury or involves using or exhibiting a deadly weapon. It is generally a second-degree felony. It becomes a first-degree felony in certain cases, such as when a deadly weapon is used against a family member causing serious bodily injury or against a public servant.

A deadly weapon finding has major consequences: judges cannot place you on regular probation, and parole eligibility is delayed. Anything can be a deadly weapon depending on how it was used, which makes the specific facts critical. Our affiliated family firm has obtained multiple dismissals of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon charges.

---

## Deadly Weapon Findings
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/violent-crimes/deadly-weapon/

What a deadly weapon finding means in Texas criminal cases and how to fight it.

A deadly weapon is a firearm, anything designed to cause death or serious injury, or anything that in its manner of use or intended use is capable of causing death or serious bodily injury. Vehicles, bats, and even shod feet have qualified.

When a jury or judge makes an affirmative deadly weapon finding, the case becomes a "3g" offense: the judge cannot grant regular community supervision, and a person sentenced to prison must generally serve half the sentence before becoming parole eligible. Contesting the finding can matter as much as contesting guilt.

---

## Disorderly Conduct & Deadly Conduct
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/violent-crimes/disorderly-conduct-deadly-conduct/

Disorderly conduct and deadly conduct charges in Texas: penalties and defenses.

Disorderly conduct covers behavior such as offensive language or gestures in public, fighting, making unreasonable noise, or displaying a firearm in a manner calculated to alarm. Most forms are Class C misdemeanors, while firearm-related forms are Class B.

Deadly conduct is more serious. Recklessly placing another in imminent danger of serious bodily injury, including pointing a gun at someone, is a Class A misdemeanor. Knowingly discharging a firearm at or in the direction of people, a home, or a vehicle is a third-degree felony.

---

## Assault on a Public Servant
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/violent-crimes/public-servant/

Assault on a public servant or peace officer charges in Houston and Fort Bend County.

Assault causing bodily injury to a person the actor knows is a public servant lawfully discharging an official duty, or in retaliation for that duty, is at least a third-degree felony. Public servants include police officers, jailers, teachers, and government employees.

These cases often arise from chaotic arrests where officers' accounts differ from video. We examine whether the officer was acting lawfully, whether the contact was intentional, and whether injuries are documented. Our affiliated family firm has obtained dismissals of assault on a peace officer and retaliation charges, and deferred probation in another case where the prior offer was prison time.

---

## Harassment of a Public Servant
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/violent-crimes/harassment-of-a-public-servant/

Harassment of a public servant charges in Texas involving bodily fluids: third-degree felony defense.

Harassment by persons in certain facilities, and harassment of a public servant, involve causing a public servant to contact blood, saliva, urine, or other bodily fluids with intent to assault, harass, or alarm. It is a third-degree felony.

These charges often arise during arrest or in jail. Intent is central. Coughing, sneezing, or accidental contact during a struggle is not the same as an intentional act.

---

## Robbery & Aggravated Robbery
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/violent-crimes/robbery/

Robbery and aggravated robbery charges in Houston: second- and first-degree felony defense.

Robbery is committing theft while intentionally, knowingly, or recklessly causing bodily injury, or threatening or placing someone in fear of imminent injury or death. It is a second-degree felony. Aggravated robbery, which involves serious bodily injury, a deadly weapon, or an elderly or disabled victim, is a first-degree felony and a "3g" offense.

Identification is often the central issue. Eyewitness identification is error-prone, especially under stress and when a weapon is present. We examine lineup procedures, video, cell-site data, and forensic evidence. A client of our affiliated family firm was acquitted of all aggravated robbery charges.

---

## Kidnapping
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/violent-crimes/kidnapping/

Kidnapping and aggravated kidnapping charges in Harris and Fort Bend County.

Kidnapping is intentionally or knowingly abducting another person, which requires restraint plus intent to prevent liberation by secreting them or by using or threatening deadly force. It is a third-degree felony. Aggravated kidnapping involves additional intent, such as holding someone for ransom or to facilitate another felony, and is a first-degree felony, reduced to second-degree if the defendant voluntarily released the victim in a safe place.

Many kidnapping allegations grow out of domestic disputes or custody disagreements, where intent and context are crucial.

---

## Unlawful Restraint
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/violent-crimes/unlawful-restraint/

Unlawful restraint charges in Texas: misdemeanor and felony levels and defenses.

Unlawful restraint means intentionally or knowingly restricting another person's movements without consent by force, intimidation, or deception, or by confining them. It is generally a Class A misdemeanor, a state jail felony when the person restrained is a child under 17, and a third-degree felony when the actor recklessly exposes the victim to a substantial risk of serious bodily injury or restrains a public servant.

A relative of a child who restrains them without force or intent to harm may have a defense.

---

## Terroristic Threat
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/violent-crimes/terroristic-threats/

Terroristic threat charges in Houston and Fort Bend County: what counts and how to defend.

A terroristic threat is threatening violence against a person or property with intent to cause a reaction by emergency officials, place someone in fear of imminent serious bodily injury, or disrupt a building, public place, or public service. A basic threat against a person is a Class B misdemeanor, a Class A misdemeanor when made against a family member or public servant, and a felony when it disrupts public services or a school.

Words spoken in anger, sarcasm, or jest, especially online, are often treated as threats after the fact. Context, intent, and the First Amendment all matter. Our affiliated family firm has obtained the dismissal of a family-household terroristic threat charge.

---

## Stalking
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/violent-crimes/stalking/

Stalking charges in Texas: third-degree felony penalties, protective orders and defenses.

Stalking under Penal Code § 42.072 requires conduct on more than one occasion, directed at a specific person, that the actor knows the other will regard as threatening and that would cause a reasonable person to fear harm or feel harassed. It is a third-degree felony, and a second-degree felony with a prior stalking conviction.

Stalking cases usually involve a history between the parties, and the evidence often consists of texts, call logs, and social media. We collect the full communication record, which frequently shows mutual contact or context that undercuts the allegation.

---

## Online Harassment & Cyberstalking
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/violent-crimes/cyberstalking/

Online harassment, cyberbullying and cyberstalking charges in Texas.

Texas prosecutes electronic harassment under Penal Code § 42.07, including repeated electronic communications meant to harass, annoy, alarm, abuse, torment, or embarrass. Most forms are Class B misdemeanors. When the conduct is repeated and threatening, prosecutors may charge stalking, a felony, based on online behavior.

Digital evidence can be spoofed, misattributed, or taken out of context. We examine account ownership, IP data, and the complete message history, and we evaluate free-speech issues.

---

## Manslaughter
URL: https://www.pinkdefense.com/violent-crimes/manslaughter/

Manslaughter and criminally negligent homicide charges in Harris and Fort Bend County.
